demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Mateo describes his hands as the one thing he used to be able to trust. Before the accident, they were his livelihood, steady and capable. He speaks with a quiet pride about his first year as an HVAC technician, about the satisfaction of diagnosing a faulty compressor or neatly soldering a copper line. He liked the physicality of the work, the tangible results. He was the guy who could fix things.

That was six months ago. Now, when he looks at his hands, he sees the moment the heavy-duty pipe wrench slipped.

It was a brutally hot July afternoon, the kind of day his company had been slammed with calls. He was on a commercial rooftop, working on a large condenser unit with Leo, a new apprentice who was shadowing him. Mateo was showing him how to torque a valve, explaining the pressure, the feel of it. He remembers the sweat dripping into his eyes, the blinding glare of the sun off the metal housing. For a split second, his grip faltered. The wrench, heavy and solid, slipped from his grasp, spun off the edge of the unit, and fell three stories.

Mateo says the sound is what he can’t forget. Not Leo’s cry, but the sickening, hollow thud that came first. When he scrambled to the edge of the roof and looked down, his world fractured. The image of Leo on the concrete below, the unnatural angle of his leg, the blood beginning to pool, is burned into his mind. He’ll be watching TV with his mother when the glint of a knife in the kitchen sends him right back to that rooftop, the sun in his eyes, the weight of the wrench gone from his hand.

In the first few weeks, he was numb. He went through the motions of the company’s investigation, the hospital visits. He sat in the waiting room while Leo underwent surgery for a shattered femur and a severe concussion. He tried to speak to Leo’s parents, but the look in their eyes—a mixture of grief and accusation—felt like a physical blow. They didn’t yell, but their quiet devastation confirmed the single thought that had taken root in his mind: *This is your fault.*

He tried to go back to work a month later, but it was impossible. The familiar rattle of tools in the truck made his stomach clench. Standing on a ladder, he was paralyzed by a dizzying wave of panic, convinced he would drop something, that he would hurt someone else. His boss was patient at first, but Mateo started calling in sick, unable to face the responsibility. His tool belt, once a source of pride, now sits in a dusty heap in the corner of his bedroom, covered by an old sheet as if it were a corpse.

Now, Mateo’s world has shrunk to the walls of his family’s small apartment. He spends most of his days in his room, the blinds drawn. Sleep offers little escape; he often jolts awake, heart pounding, the image of Leo’s fall replaying in vivid detail. He is perpetually on edge. The sound of a car backfiring or a dish dropping sends a jolt of adrenaline through him, his body tensing for a disaster he feels is always imminent. He avoids his old friends, convinced he is a source of bad luck, a danger to be around. He feels a profound sense of alienation from his family, who try to coax him out, their worried expressions only deepening his shame. He feels broken, not in the way an air conditioner is broken—something that can be diagnosed and fixed—but in a fundamental, irreparable way. He just wants the noise in his head to stop, but the echo of that thud on the pavement never seems to fade.
